newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran troops muster for Gulf wargames.
newsitem.headline: Iran troops muster for Gulf wargames.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of revolutionary troops mustered in four Iranian provinces on Tuesday for Gulf wargames to train for surprise attacks on "enemies" posing threats to the Islamic Republic.

Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei arrived in the port of Bandar Abbas overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, conduit for half the world's oil exports, to watch the start on Tuesday evening of three days of amphibious military exercises.
Some 200,000 troops -- Revolutionary Guards and paramilitary Basij volunteers -- were to take part in the wargames, Iran's official news agency IRNA reported from the scene.
Iran's southern coastline runs the length of the Gulf, through which about 15 million barrels of oil -- equal to Europe's daily consumption -- pass every day.
It said Khamenei, commander-in-chief of Iran's half-million-strong armed forces, arrived in the city to a warm welcome from local officials and people.

Chants in his support echoed in the city's Qods (Jerusalem) mosque on his arrival, the agency said. Streets were decorated with banners, posters of Khamenei's predecessor, the Islamic Republic's founder the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the Iranian tricolour and colourful lights.
IRNA quoted the guards' deputy commander, Brigadier General Rahim Safavi, as saying 200,000 troops would take part in the exercises code-named "Tariq-ol Qods" (Road to Jerusalem).

They were to test surface-to-air, shore-to-sea and surface-to-surface missiles, Safavi said, adding that Revolutionary Guard experts and engineers had the technical know-how to build various missiles.

IRNA quoted him as saying Iran, which regularly holds wargames in the Gulf, wanted "to upgrade the quality of its personnel so that it can better defend Islamic ideals and safeguard territorial integrity".

He stressed that security in the Gulf was a collective responsibility "of all regional countries and as such Iran is holding the Tariq-ol Qods manoeuvres as a step to demonstrate its prowess for guaranteeing Persian Gulf security".

He said Iran would not allow any "alien power to destabilise regional security". Safavi said the departure of "intruding forces" -- a term often used to describe U.S. forces in the Gulf -- would help enhance cooperation among regional states.
In the Iranian capital, the Tehran Times newspaper called on Iran's Gulf Arab neighbours to increase cooperation and conclude a regional security pact encompassing all regional countries.

The six Arab oil states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman and the United Arab Emirates -- have been leery of overtures from Iran, whose 60 million people outnumbers them by more than two to one.
They have accused the Islamic Republic of interfering in the internal affairs of GCC states and the UAE is in dispute with Iran over three islands near the entrance to the Gulf.
The English-language daily referred to remarks on Monday by Major-General Mohsen Rezaei, the Revolutionary Guards' commander, that Iran was ready to conclude a security pact with the Gulf states.
"It is time the Arabs realised that their security can best be protected through peaceful coexistence with Iran," it said, adding that this was not possible without cooperation.
A regional security pact would minimise and gradually eradicate dependence on foreign powers, Tehran Times added.
